title: How I Started Learning Programming
excerpt: Programming wasn't something I planned to study. It began with curiosity, a desire to understand how technology works, and a decision that eventually led me to study Informatics.
content:
Programming wasn't something I planned to study. Growing up, I was more familiar with numbers and formulas than with code. My path into mathematics and physics competitions during senior high school taught me how to think logically and solve problems—but I never imagined that those same skills would lead me toward Informatics.

When I finally enrolled as an Informatics student and sat down to write my first lines of C, I remember feeling a strange mix of excitement and confusion. The syntax looked nothing like the equations I was used to, and my first program didn't even compile. I stared at the error message for a long time before realizing I had simply forgotten a semicolon.

That mistake, small as it was, taught me something important: programming rewards patience more than talent. Every error was a lesson, not a failure. Slowly, C started to make sense. Then C++ followed, and eventually Python, each language teaching me a slightly different way of thinking about problems.

What kept me going wasn't the promise of a career or a good grade. It was the small moment when a program finally ran correctly after hours of debugging—that feeling of things clicking into place. It's the same feeling that still motivates me today, whether I'm fixing a bug in a website or learning a completely new framework.

Looking back, I think that first frustrating semicolon error was the real beginning of my journey—not the moment I chose Informatics, but the moment I decided not to give up on it.

title: Building My First Java Project
excerpt: This wasn't a tutorial. It was my first real attempt at building something from scratch—a Library Management System that taught me more than any lecture could.
content:
By 2025, I had learned enough programming fundamentals to feel confident—until I actually tried to build something real. My first serious project was a Library Management System built in Java, and it humbled me almost immediately.

The idea seemed simple on paper: let a librarian add books, register members, and track borrowing. But turning that idea into working software meant dealing with things no tutorial had fully prepared me for—designing a database structure that actually made sense, handling edge cases like a member trying to borrow a book that was already checked out, and untangling bugs that only appeared after hours of use.

The hardest part wasn't the code itself, but the decisions behind it. Should a book's status be tracked in its own table or as a simple flag? What happens if two actions happen at nearly the same time? These weren't questions with a single right answer, and figuring that out taught me to think less like someone following instructions and more like someone designing a system.

There were plenty of frustrating nights spent chasing a bug that turned out to be a single misplaced condition. But by the time the project was finished, I understood object-oriented programming in a way that no classroom explanation had achieved. I had built something that worked, end to end, because I designed it—not because I copied it.

That project became a turning point. It was the first time I felt like a developer instead of a student memorizing syntax.

title: Why I Created This Personal Website
excerpt: I could have built a portfolio instead. I chose to build something more personal—a place to document who I am, not just what I've made.
content:
When I decided to build a website about myself, the obvious choice would have been a portfolio—a clean grid of projects meant to impress recruiters. Instead, I chose to build something different: a personal website that tells the story of who I am, not just a list of what I've built.

The distinction matters more than it might seem. A portfolio answers the question "what can this person build?" A personal website answers a different question: "who is this person, and how did they get here?" I wanted a space where my journey—moving between cities, discovering competitions, struggling through my first lines of code—could exist alongside my technical growth, not be erased by it.

That's also why I eventually decided to keep this site separate from my portfolio. Each has its own purpose. This website is where I reflect, document, and grow in public. My portfolio, hosted separately, is where the proof of that growth lives in the form of real projects. Together, they tell a fuller story than either could alone.

Building this site has also been a project in itself—choosing a color palette, writing every section by hand, deciding what to include and what to leave out. It forced me to think carefully about how I want to be understood, not just by recruiters, but by anyone who stumbles across it, including my own family.

If you're reading this, you're not just looking at a list of my skills. You're reading the story of how I became someone who builds things—and that, to me, is worth far more than a portfolio alone could ever show.

title: Learning Beyond the Classroom
excerpt: University gave me a foundation. Everything I've built beyond that came from documentation, late-night debugging, open-source communities, and countless hours of self-learning.
content:
University gave me a solid foundation—algorithms, databases, the fundamentals of software engineering. But most of what I actually use day to day, I learned outside the classroom.

A lot of that learning happened through official documentation. Early on, I avoided it, preferring quick tutorials that promised fast results. Over time, I realized tutorials teach you to follow, while documentation teaches you to understand. Reading through Laravel's docs or a library's README taught me not just how to use a tool, but why it was designed that way.

Open-source projects and GitHub became another classroom of sorts. Browsing through other people's code—sometimes messy, sometimes elegant—showed me patterns and approaches I would never have thought of on my own. I didn't need to contribute to learn from them; simply reading real-world code was often more instructive than any assignment.

Online communities and even AI tools like ChatGPT became part of this process too, not as a shortcut, but as a way to ask better questions and get unstuck faster when documentation alone wasn't enough. The goal was never to have someone else do the thinking for me, but to reduce the time between being stuck and understanding why.

What ties all of this together is a simple belief: formal education starts the process, but it was never meant to finish it. The moment I stopped treating learning as something that only happens in a classroom, I started growing a lot faster.

title: Why I Want to Become a Software Engineer
excerpt: Not because it's a trending career, but because software gives me the opportunity to turn ideas into solutions that can genuinely help people.
content:
People sometimes ask why I chose software engineering, expecting an answer about salaries or job demand. The honest answer is simpler: I chose it because building things that solve real problems is one of the few things I've done that never feels like work, even when it's difficult.

I still remember the first time I built something that someone outside my family actually used—a small web-based system for a client. Watching them navigate something I had built, something that made a small part of their life easier, felt different from any grade or certificate I had earned before. It wasn't about being praised for skill. It was about being useful.

Software engineering also appeals to me because it rewards curiosity. There is always a new framework, a new pattern, a new problem to understand—Web3, UI/UX, automation, backend architecture. I don't see this as overwhelming; I see it as a career that will never run out of things to learn, which suits someone who has never really enjoyed standing still.

There's also a quieter reason. Coming from a family that valued discipline and hard work, I wanted a path where consistent effort could clearly translate into real results—where getting a little better every day eventually adds up to something meaningful. Software development, with its endless small problems to solve, gave me exactly that kind of path.

I don't know exactly what kind of software engineer I'll become—Full-Stack, Web3, or something that doesn't have a name yet. But I know the reason I'm walking this path isn't trend or convenience. It's the simple, repeated feeling of turning an idea into something real.
